--- title: "Einführung in R und Quarto" subtitle: "Data Frames & Tibbles" author: "Andreas Haupt" bibliography: IntRo.bib format: revealjs: theme: style.scss css: global.css slideNumber: true fig-align: center editor: source execute: echo: false message: false warning: false --- --- ## Some vectors ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 34 22 42 12 76 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] Europe Africa Africa Asia S. America Levels: Africa Asia Australia Europe N. America S. America ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] FALSE TRUE TRUE TRUE TRUE ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Agnes" "Martin" "Hakan" "Tu" "Thais" ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1 0 3 0 4 ``` ::: ::: ## {background-image="http://www.europeansocialsurvey.org/about/news/img/round7.png"} ::: {.centered} **Data Frames** ::: ## Data frames **Data frames** organize vectors of *equal length* along their indices. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` name age conti employed nr_kids 1 Agnes 34 Europe FALSE 1 2 Martin 22 Africa TRUE 0 3 Hakan 42 Africa TRUE 3 4 Tu 12 Asia TRUE 0 5 Thais 76 S. America TRUE 4 ``` ::: ::: . . . ::: {.centered} Data frames are the typical "rectangular" way to organize data: ::: ![](https://d33wubrfki0l68.cloudfront.net/6f1ddb544fc5c69a2478e444ab8112fb0eea23f8/91adc/images/tidy-1.png){width="60%"} ## {background-image="http://www.europeansocialsurvey.org/about/news/img/round7.png"} ![](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rstudio/hex-stickers/master/PNG/tibble.png){width="30%"} ## Tibbles **Tibbles** are data frames. But they have some improved features, so we will work with them. ::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` name age conti employed nr_kids 1 Agnes 34 Europe FALSE 1 2 Martin 22 Africa TRUE 0 3 Hakan 42 Africa TRUE 3 4 Tu 12 Asia TRUE 0 5 Thais 76 S. America TRUE 4 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 5 × 5 name age conti employed nr_kids 1 Agnes 34 Europe FALSE 1 2 Martin 22 Africa TRUE 0 3 Hakan 42 Africa TRUE 3 4 Tu 12 Asia TRUE 0 5 Thais 76 S. America TRUE 4 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Address single variables (The `$` operator) ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] Europe Africa Africa Asia S. America Levels: Africa Asia Australia Europe N. America S. America ``` ::: ::: . . . ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Min. 1st Qu. Median Mean 3rd Qu. Max. 12.0 22.0 34.0 37.2 42.0 76.0 ``` ::: ::: . . . ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Africa Asia Australia Europe N. America S. America 2 1 0 1 0 1 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.centered} Wait, why does `summary()` give me first some summary statistics and then a frequency table? ::: ## `select()` several variables ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 5 × 2 name nr_kids 1 Agnes 1 2 Martin 0 3 Hakan 3 4 Tu 0 5 Thais 4 ``` ::: ::: ## `select()` several variables `select()` has a couple of nice **helper functions**, see `?select` for details. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 5 × 2 name nr_kids 1 Agnes 1 2 Martin 0 3 Hakan 3 4 Tu 0 5 Thais 4 ``` ::: ::: ## `filter()` cases (Based on values in certain variables) ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 5 name age conti employed nr_kids 1 Martin 22 Africa TRUE 0 2 Hakan 42 Africa TRUE 3 ``` ::: ::: . . . ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 5 name age conti employed nr_kids 1 Martin 22 Africa TRUE 0 2 Hakan 42 Africa TRUE 3 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.centered} Why is there a `,` after `"Africa"`? ::: ## Index (Rows, and columns) In contrast to vectors, data frames and tibbles have rows and columns. As in matrix algebra, R's index thus distinguishes `[rows, columns]`. The `,` after `"Africa"` tells R that we talk about rows. To understand how the index method works, remember logical vectors: ::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] Europe Africa Africa Asia S. America Levels: Africa Asia Australia Europe N. America S. America ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] FALSE TRUE TRUE FALSE FALSE ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 5 name age conti employed nr_kids 1 Martin 22 Africa TRUE 0 2 Hakan 42 Africa TRUE 3 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} . . . ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 5 × 6 name age conti employed nr_kids selector 1 Agnes 34 Europe FALSE 1 FALSE 2 Martin 22 Africa TRUE 0 TRUE 3 Hakan 42 Africa TRUE 3 TRUE 4 Tu 12 Asia TRUE 0 FALSE 5 Thais 76 S. America TRUE 4 FALSE ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Transform, recode & generate (Variables of tibbles) To transform and recode simply use `$` to clarify which tibble you are referring to. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] -3.2 -15.2 4.8 -25.2 38.8 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] Europe Afrika! Afrika! Asia S. America Levels: Afrika! Asia Australia Europe N. America S. America ``` ::: ::: . . . If you rather want to generate a new variable, just give it a name. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] -0.1305090 -0.6199178 0.1957635 -1.0277584 1.5824217 ``` ::: ::: ## Transform, recode & generate (Several variables of a tibble) If you want to transform and recode several variables from the same tibble, get used to use `mutate()`. ::: {.note} You will better understand why in Session 6 on piping! ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 5 × 8 name age conti employed nr_kids selector z_age z_nr_kids 1 Agnes -3.20 Europa! FALSE -0.6 FALSE -0.131 -0.330 2 Martin -15.2 Afrika! TRUE -1.6 TRUE -0.620 -0.881 3 Hakan 4.8 Afrika! TRUE 1.4 TRUE 0.196 0.771 4 Tu -25.2 Asien! TRUE -1.6 FALSE -1.03 -0.881 5 Thais 38.8 S. America TRUE 2.4 FALSE 1.58 1.32 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.note} Also, look how RStudio structures the brackets. It helps you to understand, within which function things are happening. ::: ## Conditional transform & recode ((i.e., for filtered cases)) To transform/recode only among certain cases, use `case_when()`. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 5 × 8 name age conti employed nr_kids selector z_age z_nr_kids 1 Agnes -3.20 Europa! FALSE -0.6 FALSE -0.131 -0.330 2 Martin -15.2 Antarctica TRUE -1.6 TRUE -0.620 -0.881 3 Hakan 4.8 Afrika! TRUE 1.4 TRUE 0.196 0.771 4 Tu -25.2 Antarctica TRUE -1.6 FALSE -1.03 -0.881 5 Thais 38.8 S. America TRUE 2.4 FALSE 1.58 1.32 ``` ::: ::: ## Conditional transform & recode ((i.e., for filtered cases)) ::: {.cell} ::: The three lines of this `case_when()` application do the following thing: 1. For all non-employed African cases ~ recode conti to "Atlantis". 2. For all those who're younger than 0 and have less than -1 kids ~ recode conti to "Antarctica". 3. All remaining cases ~ use their original conti values, but transform them to a character vector. - Remember, R is class sensitive! It will not combine numeric information into a character vector. Because we give `case_when()` `"Atlantis"` and `"Antarctica"` as new values, it assumes that we want to make conti a character vector. Thus we cannot supply the former factor values (which are integer) in line three. ## `case_when()` and `NA` ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 5 × 8 name age conti employed nr_kids selector z_age z_nr_kids 1 Agnes -3.20 FALSE -0.6 FALSE -0.131 -0.330 2 Martin -15.2 Antarctica TRUE -1.6 TRUE -0.620 -0.881 3 Hakan 4.8 TRUE 1.4 TRUE 0.196 0.771 4 Tu -25.2 Antarctica TRUE -1.6 FALSE -1.03 -0.881 5 Thais 38.8 TRUE 2.4 FALSE 1.58 1.32 ``` ::: ::: In R vectors are type sensitive; the elements of one vector may only be of one type. If you type `?NA`, you will learn: > "*NA is a logical* constant of length 1 which contains a missing value indicator. *NA can be coerced to any other vector type* except raw." ## `case_when()` and `NA` `NA` are type sensitive, too! Therefore, coerce NA to character/numeric with `as.character()`/`as.numeric()`. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 5 × 8 name age conti employed nr_kids selector z_age z_nr_kids 1 Agnes -3.20 FALSE -0.6 FALSE -0.131 -0.330 2 Martin -15.2 Antarctica TRUE -1.6 TRUE -0.620 -0.881 3 Hakan 4.8 TRUE 1.4 TRUE 0.196 0.771 4 Tu -25.2 Antarctica TRUE -1.6 FALSE -1.03 -0.881 5 Thais 38.8 TRUE 2.4 FALSE 1.58 1.32 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.note} Alternatively, you can also use type-specific `NA`: `NA_character_`, `NA_real_`, etc.. ::: ## {background-image="http://www.europeansocialsurvey.org/docs/img/general_banner.jpg"} ::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.centered} Please register as a user: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ![](https://encrypted-tbn0.gstatic.com/images?q=tbn:ANd9GcQc8K5da5GSR5c4x4lJBIaBheKgcqfNjFfihonLBJWqbzUYVitp&s){width="50%"} ::: ::: ## Import downloaded data The classic way to work with actual data, is to download them to some folder and to then import them to your software environment. The tidyverse contains the following three packages: ::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} ![](https://haven.tidyverse.org/logo.png){width="30%"} - The "haven" package allows you to import Stata, SPSS, and SAS files. ::: {.note} See the respective [Haven Website](https://haven.tidyverse.org/). ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} ![](https://readr.tidyverse.org/logo.png){width="65%"} ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ![](https://readxl.tidyverse.org/logo.png){width="65%"} ::: ::: - The "readr" package allows you to import csv, tsv and fwf files.
::: {.note} See the respective [Readr Website](https://readr.tidyverse.org/) and [Cheat Sheet](https://rawgit.com/rstudio/cheatsheets/master/data-import.pdf). ::: - The readxl package allows you to read in Excel's xlsx files. ::: {.note} See the respective [Readxl Website](https://readxl.tidyverse.org/). ::: ::: ::: ## Importing the ESS via the ESS API Beware, however, that using an API assumes you have internet access! It thus makes sense to have an extra R-Script for Data import and transformation, and then other ones for data analyses and visualization. ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ## First steps with the ESS ::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} ![](images/dscrgrp-dataframes.png){width="100%"} ::: {.cell} ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} . . . ::: {.centered} Not very telling...
But remember, R does not do labels,
in contrast to Stata or SPSS! ::: ![](https://i.vimeocdn.com/portrait/3399477_300x300){width="40%"} ::: ::: ## Importing labelled data! ::: {.column width="50%"} R imports Stata and SPSS labels, but cannot handle them. Thus, when you import Stata or SPSS data,
... you need to change each labelled variable to **numeric or factor** from the outset of your analysis!! ::: ## Importing labelled data! ::: {.column width="50%"} If you want to use a variable as categorical, use `as_factor()` to make the labels the new factor levels: ::: {.cell} ::: ::: ## Importing labelled data! ::: {.column width="50%"} If you want to use a variable as numeric, use `zap_labels()` to prohibit problems with the imported labels: ::: {.cell} ::: ::: --- ## Today's general lessons 1. *Data frames* organize equally-sized vectors along their indices; *Tibbles* are modernized data frames. The indices of data frames/tibbles are organized as `[row, column]`. 2. *Helper functions* are sub-functions that help you to make coding easier in many ways. They only work within the confines of the function for which they were designed as helpers. 3. Addressing variables means to address the columns of a data frame. Filtering cases means to address certain rows. Both is possible via the index `[row, column]`, but the `filter()` and `select()` functions have advantages. 4. R has no labels. The idea is that numeric variables have a scale (e.g., cm, years, DKK), while categorical variables have no true representation in numbers. When you import labelled data from Stata or SPSS, the labels are stored in R but will create confusion in the mid run. Make sure to `zap_labels()` from numeric variables and to treat categorical variables `as_factor()`. ## Today's important operators 1. `$`: Allows your to address vectors contained in a data frame/tibble. ## Today's (important) functions 1. `data.frame()`: organize several vectors of equal length by their index. 2. `as_tibble()`: take a data frame and make it a Tibble. 3. `summary()`: Give a summary of an object. 4. `select()`: select several variables from a data frame/Tibble. 5. `filter()`: filter cases based on values in certain variables. 6. `mutate()`: Adds new variables and preserves existing. Good for recoding several variables. 7. `case_when()`: Conditional recode for cases filtered in complex ways. 8. `as_factor()`: Make a labelled Stata/SPSS variable a factor. 9. `zap_labels()`: Make a labelled Stata/SPSS variable numeric. ## Literatur ::: {#refs} :::

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
